newsitem.title: UK: Fashanu not guilty of match-fixing, says lawyer.
newsitem.headline: Fashanu not guilty of match-fixing, says lawyer.

text.p: The lawyer for former Wimbledon striker John Fashanu on Monday denied his client was guilty of fixing soccer matches and said there was absolutely no evidence to suggest he was corrupt.
Trevor Burke told a court that the prosecution had failed to prove Fashanu was involved in any attempt to fix matches for an Asian betting syndicate.

"The case against Fashanu is the weakest of all," said Burke, noting that the striker -- Wimbledon's top scorer for six consecutive seasons -- had not been accused of actually underperforming on the field.

"The Crown (prosecution) did not find a single incident worthy of you to consider by playing frame-by-frame film to show Fashanu missing an open goal, conceding a penalty or making a dreadful backpass which allowed the opposition to score a goal," he said.

Fashanu and Malaysian businessman Heng Suan Lim are accused of passing cash from the betting syndicate to former Liverpool goalkeeper Bruce Grobbelaar and ex-Wimbledon keeper Hans Segers to fix matches by letting in goals.
Lim admits he paid the two goalkeepers to forecast the results of matches but all four deny rigging games.

Bank statements showed Lim and Fashanu received huge sums of money from the Far East -- much of it from wealthy Indonesian cocoa trader and gambler Johannes Josef -- which the prosecution said neither man had been able to explain away.

But Burke said Fashanu and Josef were business partners, investing in a duty-free shop at Lagos airport and other ventures. Josef had sent Lim 150,000 pounds ($244,200) before the Malaysian met a single soccer player, he added.

Burke said the key to dismissing the charges against Fashanu was three games between Wimbledon and Liverpool in 28 days at the end of 1993, a time when the prosecution says the match- fixing gang was in full swing.
The Asian syndicates -- which won the largest amounts by betting on teams to either lose or win -- stood to pick up a fortune by ensuring Wimbledon lost, Burke said.

"Imagine the very best Christmas present for corrupt gamblers...you have three bent players in the same match. You could have Fashanu fluffing them up front and Segers dribbling them in at the back," he said.

The first game, a cup match, was drawn, and Wimbledon won the replay on penalties after another draw. The third match, a league game, also ended in a draw. Grobbelaar, Fashanu and Segers played in all three games.

"These matches weren't fixed...there were no calls to Indonesia in this period when you would expect the phone lines to be the busiest they had ever been. This is a very very powerful point for the defence," said Burke.
The prosecution concentrated on the flurry of phone calls between the defendants and also to Indonesia in the run-up to matches Segers and Grobbelaar are said to have rigged.
But Burke said the records of phone calls were misleading, because they showed 60 percent of Lim's calls to Indonesia had been made before he met either goalkeeper.
In the 50 months between the defendants' first meeting each other and their arrest, Fashanu called Segers 99 times and Grobbelaar 54 times.
"But in the same period he called Aston Villa goalkeeper Mark Bosnich 228 times...and there is no suggestion Bosnich is corrupt," Burke told the court. ($1=.6142 Pound)
